848.title: Mata Sundari's letters
848.hook: her hukamnamas guided the scattered sangats in these years
848.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Mata Sundari as a guiding presence for the Khalsa after Guru Gobind Singh, and hukamnamas, letters of instruction, are still issued from the Akal Takht and read aloud in gurdwaras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two slips of paper in the Amritsar pool, and two Khalsas who agreed how to decide before they knew the answer. Your line was settle it fairly. Today, the woman who sent the man at the pool.

A rider arrives at a village after days on the road, carrying a folded letter. The sangat, the local gathering of Sikhs, comes together to hear it read aloud. Someone opens it carefully. It begins with a blessing. It names them. It tells them to keep the Guru's way, to stay together, to send what help they can. Then it's folded again and kept. There was no Guru in a human body anymore. The Khalsa was scattered and hunted. And from Delhi, a widow was writing letters.
screen: `A RIDER WITH A FOLDED LETTER.` → `THE SANGAT GATHERS TO HEAR IT.` → `A WIDOW IN DELHI, WRITING.`

segments.voice: Mata Sundari was the wife of Guru Gobind Singh. After the Guru passed, Sikhs believe the Guruship rested in the scripture and the Khalsa together, so no one would sit on the Guru's seat again. But people still needed someone to hear their questions, to steady them, to say keep going. Tradition says that role fell, in large part, to her. She lived in Delhi, and from there she wrote hukamnamas. A hukamnama is a letter of instruction, an order given with authority and love at the same time. The Gurus had written them before her; now the letters went out in her name to sangats in villages and towns far away. Tradition remembers them asking sangats to keep to the Guru's teachings, to gather and sing, to support the community's work, and to stay united when they were pulled apart. Some tellings say she also took practical steps, sending Bhai Mani Singh to Amritsar to care for the Harmandir. So yesterday's story and today's are tied together: the man at the pool was there, tradition says, because she sent him. Here is what's striking. She held no army and no throne. She had ink, paper, riders and a name that people trusted. In a time when gathering openly could cost a life, a letter could reach a place a crowd could not. A sangat holding her hukamnama knew someone far away was thinking of them by name.

849.title: Living in the forests
849.hook: with a price on their heads, Sikhs lived on horseback in forests and deserts
849.howItsDone: Sikhs tell stories of the forest years in gurdwaras and at home, and remember them in the daily Ardas, which honors those who held to the faith through persecution.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Sundari's letters, read aloud to sangats far from Delhi. Your line was letters in hard times. Today, the people those letters were trying to reach.

A saddle for a pillow. A blanket that is also a cloak. A cooking pot tied behind, and the reins never far from your hand, even asleep. Tradition says that in these years whole Sikh families had no address at all. The governors in Lahore had put a price on a Sikh's head, and a village that sheltered them could be punished. So the Khalsa moved into the places nobody wanted to follow: thick forests along the rivers, the dry country to the south, the edges of the desert.
screen: `A SADDLE FOR A PILLOW.` → `A PRICE ON THEIR HEADS.` → `INTO THE FORESTS AND DESERTS.`

segments.voice: What did that life look like? Tradition remembers bands of horsemen, called jathas, moving from one hiding place to the next, never staying long. They ate what they could find, or what friendly villagers slipped them in the dark. They slept in shifts. When soldiers came close, they scattered and met again somewhere agreed in advance. A horse was not a possession. It was the house, the escape, the way to bring food home. And here's the surprising part: out of that hard life came humor. The Khalsa developed its own way of speaking, sometimes called Khalsa bole, the Khalsa's words, and some of it is a joke against hardship. Some tellings say a handful of dry chickpeas was called almonds. A lone rider might call himself an army. It sounds like bravado, and maybe it was. But it was also a way of refusing to let the hunt decide how they felt: the chardi kala this path met in the hills after Lohgarh, turned into a joke. The Gurus' hymns were with them too. Riders who knew them by heart could recite the morning and evening prayers in a forest clearing as easily as in a town. A gurdwara needs walls. The Name, the tradition says, does not. Where the riders stopped, the sangat was. Some readers hear one more thing in these stories: a reminder that a roof, a bed and a door that locks are not ordinary at all.

850.title: Bota Singh and Garja Singh
850.hook: tradition says two Sikhs set up a toll on the highway to prove the Khalsa was still alive
850.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bota Singh and Garja Singh as a picture of chardi kala, high spirits under persecution, and it is often retold in gurdwara talks and children's classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, life in the forests, with a saddle for a pillow. Your line was home was a horse. Today, a quiet story with a loud ending.

Two travelers pass a clump of bushes by the road. They glimpse a man hiding there, and one says to the other, loud enough to be heard: that can't be a Sikh. The Sikhs are finished. And if any were left, they wouldn't hide. Tradition says the man in the bushes was Bota Singh, and that sentence stung him more than any sword.
screen: `A MAN HIDING BY THE ROAD.` → `THE SIKHS ARE FINISHED.` → `THEY WOULDN'T HIDE.`

segments.voice: In the hunted years, tradition says, the governor's men claimed the Khalsa had been wiped out. Bota Singh had been living rough, slipping into Amritsar at night to bathe in the sacred pool and then disappearing again. When he heard the travelers, he decided the claim needed an answer. So he and his companion Garja Singh walked out of hiding and did something almost absurd. They picked a spot on the great highway near Tarn Taran, by a roadside inn, armed themselves with heavy clubs, and set up a toll. Every cart paid a small coin; every donkey, a smaller one. And, tradition says, travelers paid. Nobody quite knew what to do with two Sikhs standing calmly in the middle of the road as if they owned it. Then Bota Singh did the boldest thing of all. He wrote a letter to the governor in Lahore, telling him who was collecting tolls on the king's highway: a message that said, in effect, still here. Soldiers were sent. The two did not run. Tradition says they fought until they fell. Notice what they were not doing. They were not stealing for themselves, and they were not trying to win a war two men could not win. They were making a point only their presence could make: the Khalsa is alive. The travelers had said a Sikh would not hide. Bota Singh and Garja Singh decided that, this once, they would not. Two clubs, a few coins, and a letter with a name on it.

851.title: The Diwali permit, 1734
851.hook: Bhai Mani Singh arranged a Diwali gathering at Amritsar, was unable to pay the tax, and was executed
851.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Mani Singh at Diwali and in the daily Ardas, which recalls those who were cut limb from limb rather than give up their faith; Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj in Lahore marks the place tradition gives for his death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bota Singh and Garja Singh, standing on the highway with a toll and a letter. Your line was still here. Today, the man from the pool returns.

Diwali at Amritsar. Lamps on the water, the Harmandir glowing, Sikhs coming in from every direction to bathe, to listen, to see each other's faces. In the hunted years, that gathering had become impossible. So a man who had served the Guru himself went to the governor in Lahore and asked, formally, for a permit. He was Bhai Mani Singh, the same Sikh who, tradition says, had once settled the quarrel of the two slips in the pool. The governor named a price, and Bhai Mani Singh agreed to pay it.
screen: `LAMPS ON THE WATER.` → `BHAI MANI SINGH ASKS FOR A PERMIT.` → `THE GOVERNOR NAMES A PRICE.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the plan was simple. Sikhs would come for Diwali, offerings would be made, and from those offerings Bhai Mani Singh would pay the fee he had promised. But word reached him that the governor meant to use the gathering as a trap, to send soldiers among the crowds. So Bhai Mani Singh did the one thing that would ruin his own position: he sent messages telling the Sikhs not to come. Think about the cost of that choice. He saved the people, and he guaranteed that the money would not be there. Few came. The offerings fell short. He could not pay. He was arrested and taken to Lahore, where, tradition says, he was offered his life if he would give up his faith. He refused. And the sentence was terrible: to be cut apart, joint by joint. Sikhs remember those who died this way. In the Ardas, the standing prayer said at the close of Sikh services, the sangat recalls those who were cut limb from limb and did not give up their faith, and tradition places Bhai Mani Singh among them. He was not only a martyr. Tradition remembers him as a scholar and scribe, a man who had served Guru Gobind Singh closely and cared for the Harmandir for years. A whole life of careful, patient service ended in one refusal. The permit was a piece of paper. What he kept was not on paper.

852.title: Nawab Kapur Singh
852.hook: offered a Mughal title, the Khalsa gave it to a man who was fanning the sangat, and he accepted humbly
852.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Nawab Kapur Singh as a lesson in seva, and gurdwara volunteers still serve the sangat in small ways, including fanning, sweeping and cleaning shoes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Diwali permit, and Bhai Mani Singh, who warned the Sikhs away and paid with his life. Your line was he kept faith. Today, a gentler scene, and a fan.

A hot day. The sangat sits together at Amritsar, and the air barely moves. At the edge of the gathering, one man stands with a large hand fan, slowly moving the air over everyone else. Nobody asked him to. It's his seva, his service. Meanwhile a messenger has arrived from Lahore with an astonishing offer from the governor: an estate, a robe of honor, and the title of Nawab, a lord. The Khalsa has to decide who, if anyone, will wear it.
screen: `A HOT DAY. A MAN WITH A FAN.` → `AN OFFER FROM LAHORE.` → `WHO WILL WEAR THE TITLE?`

segments.voice: Why would a governor who had hunted the Sikhs offer them a title? Tradition says force had not worked, so he tried another way: give them land and rank, and perhaps they would settle down and stop resisting. The Khalsa met to discuss it. Some wanted no title from the government that had killed their people; others saw a chance for a little breathing room. And the leaders who were asked to take it, tradition says, turned it down. So the gathering made a remarkable decision: the title would go to the one doing seva. They looked around, and there was Kapur Singh, still fanning the sangat. Not the loudest, not the most powerful, but the one with the fan in his hand. Kapur Singh did not grab it. Tradition says he would accept the robe of honor only after it had been touched to the feet of five respected Sikhs, as if to say the honor belonged to the Khalsa and he was only carrying it. And he asked one more thing: that being a nawab would never excuse him from his old service. Some tellings say his seva was cleaning the stables and tending the horses, and he kept at it. He went on to become a leader of the whole Khalsa, organizing it in the hard years ahead. But the story keeps the fan in its first scene. Seva means selfless service, and the tradition holds that it is the root leadership grows from, not a step to climb past.

853.title: The two Dals
853.hook: the Khalsa organized into the elders' army and the young army
853.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Budha Dal and Taruna Dal as the Khalsa's organization under Nawab Kapur Singh, and Nihang Sikh groups today still carry the name Budha Dal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nawab Kapur Singh, the man with the fan who was given a governor's title. Your line was the humble nawab. Today, what the humble nawab built.

Here is a tension that turns up in families, in teams, in congregations. The young want to move. The old want to keep. The young say: you're too careful. The old say: you're too quick. Sometimes one side wins and the other drifts away. The Khalsa, in its hard years, had both kinds of Sikh in its ranks, with real lives at stake. And tradition says that under Nawab Kapur Singh each was given a name and a job.
screen: `THE YOUNG WANT TO MOVE.` → `THE OLD WANT TO KEEP.` → `A NAME AND A JOB FOR EACH.`

segments.voice: Dal means a host, an army, a body of people moving together. Tradition says that under Nawab Kapur Singh the Khalsa was organized into two of them: the Budha Dal, the army of the elders, and the Taruna Dal, the army of the young. Each had its own work. The tellings say the Budha Dal, the older Sikhs, looked after the holy places and the steady life of the community, and gave counsel. The Taruna Dal, the younger riders, took on the fast, dangerous work of defense, moving where they were needed. Neither was the junior partner. The elders were not pushed aside as too slow; the young were not held back as too reckless. In the tellings, they were separate, but not apart. Tradition says that when the Khalsa gathered at Amritsar, both Dals came together, sat in the same sangat, and made decisions as one. The young had the elders' memory. The elders had the young's strength. And over both stood a shared allegiance: not to a Dal, but to the Guru's way. Tradition says the Taruna Dal later grew and was divided into smaller bands, and those bands, in time, became the seeds of something bigger. But today the point is simpler. A community needs its grandparents and its teenagers, the ones who remember why and the ones who can still run. The two Dals are a picture of how not to waste either.

854.title: Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh
854.hook: two Sikhs rode into Amritsar in disguise to end a desecration of the Harmandir in 1740
854.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh as a defense of the Harmandir's sanctity, and it is often recalled in gurdwara talks about the Khalsa's hard century.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the two Dals, elders and young in one sangat; your line was old and young together. This week: Mata Sundari's letters, the forests, a toll on the highway, the Diwali permit, a nawab with a fan, and the two Dals.

Far to the south, in the dry country where hunted Sikhs had taken refuge, a traveler from Amritsar arrives with news nobody wants to hear. The Harmandir, the house of the Guru at the center of the sacred pool, has been taken over by a local official. Tradition says he is using it for drinking parties and dancing, inside the place where the Guru's hymns are sung. The listeners are silent. Then two men stand up.
screen: `NEWS FROM AMRITSAR.` → `THE HARMANDIR DESECRATED.` → `TWO MEN STAND UP.`

segments.voice: The official was named Massa Ranghar, and in the tradition he becomes a picture of contempt: someone who took a holy place and filled it with exactly what it was not for. Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh decided to end it. They could not march an army into Amritsar, so they used a disguise. Tradition says they dressed as village headmen coming to pay revenue, and filled their bags with something that clinked like coins; some tellings say broken pieces of pottery, cut round. They rode into Amritsar, tied their horses outside, and walked in carrying their bags as if they had come to pay what was owed. They were let through. Inside, they found Massa Ranghar at his entertainment. Tradition says they struck him down, and were back on their horses and gone before the guards understood what had happened. The story is told with fire, and it's worth saying what the tradition sees in it. Not a love of violence. The Harmandir belongs to the Guru and to everyone who comes to it; its doors, Sikhs say, open in every direction. Using it for mockery was an attack on what it stands for. The two riders were not after loot or power. They rode in to give the place back to its purpose. A hard story, honestly told. But the image that stays is the two horses outside the gate, and two men who had every reason to stay safe in the desert, choosing not to.

If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
